after.asserts:
Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets of feature types and score bins. For each group $t\in\{1,2\}$, let $N_t>0$ be its total mass and let $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}=1$. Let $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ be the probability of the positive binary outcome $Y=1$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A randomized risk assignment consists of scores $v_b\in[0,1]$ for $b\in\mathcal B$ and a single matrix $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$ with $\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}X_{\sigma b}=1$ for each $\sigma$; conditional on feature type $\sigma$, the assignment chooses bin $b$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}$, independently of group and outcome. Thus, for a group-$t$ individual chosen according to its feature distribution, $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$, and the assigned score is $S=v_B$. The expected positive mass is $\mu_t=N_t\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$, and the group base rate is $\rho_t=\mu_t/N_t$.

The assignment is **calibrated within group $t$** if for every $b\in\mathcal B$,
$$
\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}.
$$
This cross-multiplied condition also covers bins with zero assigned mass. The instance permits perfect prediction when $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$ for every feature type with $a_{1\sigma}+a_{2\sigma}>0$; a score assignment is perfectly predictive when $S=Y$ almost surely in each group.

after.asserts:
Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets, and let $t\in\{1,2\}$ index two groups. In group $t$, feature type $\sigma$ has proportion $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$, where $\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}=1$, and total mass $N_t>0$. The positive binary outcome $Y=1$ has probability $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A common randomized assignment sends feature type $\sigma$ to bin $b\in\mathcal B$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$, where $\sum_bX_{\sigma b}=1$, independently of group and outcome; bin $b$ has score $v_b\in[0,1]$. Set $\rho_t=\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$ and $\mu_t=N_t\rho_t$. Assume $0<\mu_t<N_t$ for each group, so both outcome classes have positive mass. Define the mean score among positive outcomes and among negative outcomes in group $t$ by
$$
\alpha_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}v_b}{\rho_t},\qquad \beta_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}v_b}{1-\rho_t},
$$
where the finite group law is $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$. The assignment is **balanced for positive outcomes** if $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, and **balanced for negative outcomes** if $\beta_1=\beta_2$. These are class-conditioned mean-score criteria; they do not assert equal mean scores over whole groups or equal thresholded error rates.

after.asserts:
Fix a group $t\in\{1,2\}$ with a finite joint law $\Pr_t$ for a binary outcome $Y\in\{0,1\}$ and a score $S$ taking finitely many values in $[0,1]$, and assume $\Pr_t(Y=1)>0$ and $\Pr_t(Y=0)>0$. For each threshold $u\in[0,1]$, define the true-positive rate $\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)=\Pr_t(S\ge u\mid Y=1)$ and the false-positive rate $\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)=\Pr_t(S\ge u\mid Y=0)$. These are finite step functions and
$$
\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=1]=\int_0^1\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)\,du,\qquad \mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=0]=\int_0^1\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)\,du.
$$
The integrals are ordinary Riemann integrals of the finite step functions.

after.asserts:
Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets. In group $t\in\{1,2\}$, feature type $\sigma\in\Sigma$ has proportion $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$, where $\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}=1$, and total mass $N_t>0$. The positive binary outcome $Y=1$ has probability $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ for feature type $\sigma$, with $p_\sigma$ the same in both groups. A common randomized assignment chooses bin $b\in\mathcal B$ from feature type $\sigma$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$, where $\sum_bX_{\sigma b}=1$; this choice is independent of group and outcome. Bin $b$ has score $v_b\in[0,1]$, and $S=v_B$. Define $\rho_t=\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$ and $\mu_t=N_t\rho_t$. Assume $0<\mu_t<N_t$ for both groups. Define the positive- and negative-outcome mean scores by
$$
\alpha_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma,b}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}v_b}{\rho_t},\qquad \beta_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma,b}a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}v_b}{1-\rho_t}.
$$
Suppose $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1=\beta_2$, and the assignment is calibrated within each group, meaning
$$
\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}
$$
for every group $t$ and bin $b$, and suppose the mean score among positive outcomes is equal across groups and the mean score among negative outcomes is equal across groups. Then either $\rho_1=\rho_2$ or $S=Y$ almost surely under each group law. In the latter case, every feature type with positive mass in either group has $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$, so the instance permits perfect prediction.

after.result: With p_sigma in {0,1}, scores S=Y give alpha=1 and beta=0 in both groups even when group proportions yield base rates 1/4 and 3/4.

after.asserts: Let group 1 have two feature types $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$, each of proportion $1/2$, with outcome probabilities $p_{\sigma_1}=1/5$ and $p_{\sigma_2}=4/5$. Let group 2 have three feature types $\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_3$ with proportions $9/32,14/32,9/32$ and outcome probabilities $p_{\tau_1}=1/10$, $p_{\tau_2}=1/2$, and $p_{\tau_3}=9/10$. Each feature type is assigned deterministically to its own bin, whose score equals that type's outcome probability; this is one common feature-based assignment for both groups, with $N_1=N_2=1$. Both groups have base rate $1/2$, and the assignment is calibrated in each group with positive- and negative-outcome mean scores $17/25$ and $8/25$, respectively. At threshold $u=1/2$, the group 1 true-positive and false-positive rates are $4/5$ and $1/5$, while the group 2 rates are $151/160$ and $79/160$. At threshold $u=9/10$, group 1's two rates are $0,0$ and group 2's are $81/160,9/160$. Thus the threshold rates change with the threshold even though both class-conditioned mean-score criteria hold.

after.asserts: 1.1 Fix $k$, abbreviate $d=d_k$, $n=n_k$, and take a fixed unit $v\in\mathbb R^d$. The row products $Z_i=(G_kv)_i$ are independent $N(0,1)$ by [A1]. From [F1], $\mathbb E e^{tZ_i^2}=(1-2t)^{-1/2}$ for $t<1/2$; applying [F2] at $t=\delta/(2(1+\delta))$ gives $\mathbb P(n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i^2\ge1+\delta)\le e^{-n[\delta-\log(1+\delta)]/2}\le e^{-n\delta^2/8}$ for $0<\delta\le1$, since $\delta-\log(1+\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1+t)\,dt\ge\delta^2/4$. For $0<\delta<1$, applying [F2] at $u=\delta/(2(1-\delta))$ gives $\mathbb P(n^{-1}\sum_iZ_i^2\le1-\delta)\le e^{-n[-\delta-\log(1-\delta)]/2}\le e^{-n\delta^2/4}$, since $-\delta-\log(1-\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1-t)\,dt\ge\delta^2/2$; at $\delta=1$ this event requires all $Z_i=0$ and has probability zero. Thus $\mathbb P(|v^{\mathsf T}(G_k^{\mathsf T}G_k/n-I_d)v|>\delta)\le2e^{-n\delta^2/8}$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

after.asserts:
Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, and $y\in\mathbb R^n$. The ordinary least-squares minimizers of $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2$ are exactly the solutions of $X^{\mathsf T}X\beta=X^{\mathsf T}y$; if $\beta_0$ is one such solution, the full minimizer set is $\beta_0+\ker X$. It is a singleton if and only if the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. For every $\lambda>0$, the ridge objective $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$ has the unique minimizer
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{ridge}}=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y.$$

after.asserts:
Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ satisfy $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$, and let $y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\lambda>0$. The objective
$$\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$$
has the unique minimizer $\widehat\beta_j=S_{n\lambda}((X^{\mathsf T}y)_j)$, where $S_a(t)=\operatorname{sgn}(t)(|t|-a)_+$, $(u)_+=\max\{u,0\}$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$. Thus the threshold is $n\lambda$ under this loss normalization.

after.asserts: 1.1 For integers $n\le\lceil e^e\rceil$, set $\lambda_n=1$, and for $n>\lceil e^e\rceil$ set $\lambda_n=(\log\log n)^{-1/2}$. Since $\log\log n>1$ in the latter range and is increasing, this defines a positive non-increasing sequence. For $k\ge2$, set $N_k=\lceil e^k\rceil$, $s_k=\lceil e^{k^2}\rceil$, $n_k=\lceil5s_kk\rceil$, and $p_k=s_k+N_k$. Use the model subsequence at sample sizes $n_k$, with $\Sigma_k=I_{p_k}$, $\beta_k^*=(\mathbf1_{s_k},0_{N_k})$, $\sigma^2=1$, and $\lambda_k=\lambda_{n_k}$. Then $C_{\min}=C_{\max}=D_{\max}=\epsilon=1$, $\rho_{n_k}=1$, and $\theta_u=1$, while $\log N_k\sim k$, $\log s_k\sim k^2$, $n_k/s_k\sim5k$, and $\log\log n_k\sim2\log k$. For $\nu=1/2$, $n_k>3s_k\log N_k+s_k$ eventually; also $\lambda_k\to0$, $n_k\lambda_k^2/\log N_k\to\infty$, and $\lambda_k+\sqrt{\log s_k/n_k}\to0$, so the claimed upper hypotheses hold. [given, construct, algebra]
